power_id text
1;2 One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study. Five were excluded because they did not complete both sessions, and one was excluded because of recording issues. The final sample size was 96. Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men). Based on the effect sizes reported in previous research for vowel space expansion (ηₚ² = 0.12-0.65; Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004), we estimated that to reach 90% power for between-subject comparison, we needed 24 participants. For other variables, following Brysbaert & Stevens, (2018), an effect of ~15 ms would require about 1,600 observations per condition to reach 80% power. With 96 participants, our design yielded more than 5,100 observations for VOT and CoG in each condition (e.g., HF-home-supervised). These observation counts, which exceed the recommended threshold, provide high statistical power even accounting for potential data loss or effects smaller than 15ms (see detailed power analysis description in pre-registration (https://osf.io/yx3e7), and Data availability and Supplementary Material for details and the complete power analysis). In order to account for personality differences that could influence competence under supervision, we administered a 13-item questionnaire on personality type (Melchior & Cheek, 1990) to determine, for each participant, whether they tended to be more or less shy and show inhibition in the presence of others. Shyness was chosen as a straightforward measure of social comfort that plausibly can influence supervised speech performance, and it correlates with related constructs such as social anxiety and extraversion (Cheek & Buss, 1981). We used the ζ-Overlapping test, in R (Pastore, 2018; Pastore & Calcagnì, 2019; Perugini et al., 2024) with permutation-based inference to compare density distribution of the two groups and estimate exact p-values. This method is assumption-free and computes the exact probability of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one observed (Perugini et al., 2024). Comparing shyness scores did not yield a significant difference between supervision groups (p = .072). All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee. Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 31 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p-values > .05 No significant exclusion rate differences were found across conditions (all p-values > .05).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 240 columns across 10 data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 10 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

What we found

  • We assessed 2 R code files for reproducibility and ran them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 2 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
  • 0 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 2 did not reproduce.
  • 4 referenced inputs unavailable (0 withheld due to size).
  • 17 installable dependencies detected.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 9 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .072 Comparing shyness scores did not yield a significant difference between supervision groups (p = .072).
p-values > .05 No significant exclusion rate differences were found across conditions (all p-values > .05).
p = .053 However, in contrast to our hypothesis, HF words were produced with significantly larger vowel space than LF words.The main effect of Environment was not significant (p = .053), although vowel space was numerically larger in the lab than at home.
p = .062 The effect of the number of repetitions did not reach significance (χ²(1) = 3.47, p = .062).
p = .585 The per-condition estimates confirmed the The Environment x Voicing interaction was significant (χ²(1) = 80.11, p < .001), which indicated a longer VOT in the lab than at home for the voiceless plosives (home -lab: β = -0.124, SE = 0.014, p < .001) but not for the voiced plosives (home -lab: β = -0.009, SE = 0.016, p = .585, d = -0.02; see Dots represent participant means; circles represent model estimates ± 95% CI (back-transformed).
p = .051 The model revealed a main effect of cat_PND, with wider vowel space for words with high than with low PND (d = 0.35), and, as in the Frequency model, a non-significant effect of Environment (p = .051).
p = .162 Critically, Frequency interacted with Environment: the frequency effect was significant at home (β = 0.28, SE = 0.064, p < .001, d = 0.07) but not in the lab (β = 0.09, SE = 0.064, p = .162, d = 0.02; Holm-corrected; Figure 5).
p = .066 Frequency was not significant (p = .066) and did not interact with Environment or Supervision.
p = .464 The interaction was significant (χ²(1) = 118.18, p < .001): VOT was longer in the lab than at home for voiceless plosives (home -lab: β = -0.140, SE = 0.015, p < .001, d = -0.24) but not for voiced plosives (β = -0.012, SE = 0.016, p = .464, d = -0.02; Holm-corrected).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

To check Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

What we found

We found 2 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

Show details

We recommend checking the sentences below, and add any missing effect sizes.

For t-tests with a reported d, coherence checks yielded 2 indeterminate cases.
Although the order was counterbalanced, we assessed the PND effect (the strongest effect we observed) on vowel space at home, restricting the sample to participants who completed their home session before any laboratory exposure (N = 48): the effect remained significant in both tasks (naming: t(48) = 8.85; reading: t(48) = 6.67; both p < .001; Supplementary Material), also when restricted to the unsupervised group (N = 26), suggesting that the validity of home recordings does not depend on prior laboratory familiarity.
Although the order was counterbalanced, we assessed the PND effect (the strongest effect we observed) on vowel space at home, restricting the sample to participants who completed their home session before any laboratory exposure (N = 48): the effect remained significant in both tasks (naming: t(48) = 8.85; reading: t(48) = 6.67; both p < .001; Supplementary Material), also when restricted to the unsupervised group (N = 26), suggesting that the validity of home recordings does not depend on prior laboratory familiarity.

For metascientific articles demonstrating that effect sizes are often not reported:

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Lastly, the study did not directly manipulate experimenter presence: participants were unsupervised at home, while an experimenter was present in the lab to ensure protocol compliance, introducing a potential confound between environment and supervision.

One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study.

Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men).

All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.

Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.

In the supervised group, participants were accompanied by the same experimenter in both environment: when in the lab, they were welcomed and seated in an experimental booth equipped with a camera and microphone for technical assistance; at home, they remained observed by the experimenter via Zoom, with their camera and microphone active throughout the session.

In the home environment, participants were permitted to use any available microphone, including both laptop-integrated and externally mounted devices.

Participants were asked to respond aloud as soon as the stimulus appeared and while it was displayed on the screen.

Finally, participants completed Cheek and Melchior’s (1990) shyness questionnaire.

All participants completed both a laboratory and a home session and may thus have become familiar with the protocol.

Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study.

Ethics approval statement:

All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee.

This study was performed in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of Basque Center on Cognition, Brain, and Language.

research_questions Despite recent dramatic improvements in web technology, some criticism and prejudices toward online behavioral experiments persist. Many researchers have questioned such intrinsic limits of online approach and examined differences in the outcomes between online and onsite (lab-based) experiments (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020; Bridges et al., 2020; de Leeuw & Motz, 2016; Hilbig, 2016). Nevertheless, some recent research showed consistency and comparability between online and onsite RT measures, which suggests that online experiments can be reliably used in psycholinguistic research. On the other hand, other fields of psycholinguistics and cognitive sciences that employ other measures than RTs (e.g., speech onset times, acoustic analyses of speech) cannot yet fully rely on web-based experiments, partly, because of the lack of comparisons with traditional methods. In addition, speech production is not studied uniquely with naming latency: there is a vast part of cognitive sciences that study speech production employing acoustic analysis instead. Crucially, investigation on the adequacy of online recording of speech production for acoustic analysis purposes has apparently never been investigated in a controlled fashion. We intend to explore whether studies on speech production can be moved online by comparing online and onsite environments.
Since the literature reports that the lexical frequency effect in reading is smaller (12-15ms) than the effect in naming (45-50ms; see Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), we aim to employ both tasks to measure with finer grain size two levels of online experiments sensitivity (without directly comparing them). We expect to replicate the robust results of lexical frequency (shorter SOT for HF words vs. LF words) in both online and onsite experiments; also, both environments will elicit comparable effects in both the reading and the naming tasks. If this will be the case, we can assume that online experiments are a suitable tool for detecting both large and small latency differences and that the online solutions can be used without substantial limitations.

We will also explore the effect of lexical frequency over acoustic features in both online and onsite environments. Regarding these features, we expect to find more hyperarticulated vowels and longer consonant VOT in the LF words compared to the HF words, with no difference between online and onsite conditions. Such results on vowel hyperarticulation and VOT would be in line with previous onsite studies (Munson, 2007; Munson and Solomon, 2004; VanDam & Port, 2005), which however never employed a picture naming task to investigate the influence of lexical frequency on acoustic features. The results that explored SOT with both tasks suggest, however, that the naming task will elicit the same pattern as reading aloud. Fricative COG modification has never been investigated in relation to lexical frequency effect, thus it is an open question whether fricatives will show higher COG with LF words than HF words.

We expect to observe differences between the Supervised and the Unsupervised groups independently of the experimental environment (and possibly depending on participants personality). Because of a more relaxed circumstance, we expect that the Unsupervised group will have longer SOTs, which would be in line with Fairs & Strijker’s (2021) explanation for their results on longer latencies in online testing (see also Belletier & Camos, 2018; Palmer et al., 2019; Guerin, 1986). Accordingly, we expect a reduced difference between LF and HF words regarding vowel space and VOT duration as compared to the Supervised group. If our expectation is confirmed, we would conclude that participants’ behavior mostly depends on the supervision and future online studies should carefully take this in consideration.
In line with the idea that both unsupervised and online sessions entail less controlled environments, we might observe an interaction between Supervision*Environment factors, which would lead to longer SOT, less hyperarticulated vowels, shorter plosive VOT (and possibly lower fricative COG) in the unsupervised-online session, as compared to the other conditions (Unsup-Online > Unsup-Onsite > Superv-Online = Superv-Onsite). However, the present literature does not allow us to draw strong predictions.
study_type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
blinding For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
randomization Each participant will be randomly assigned to one of the two groups (Supervised and Unsupervised).
Within each task, the presentation order of stimuli will be randomized.
existing_data Registration prior to creation of data
sample_size Our target sample size is two groups of 48 Spanish speakers. We will attempt to recruit 100 participants assuming that there might be some technical problems or some of the participants may not complete all the sessions. All participants will be paid for their time.
We will recruit a total of 100 native speakers of Spanish, aged 18-35, with low or medium-low proficiency in any other language, to form two groups of 50 each. The two groups of participants will be matched for age, L2 proficiency and education level.
measured_variables For each trial (in both tasks) we will measure Speech Onset Time.
Based on the three vowels (/i/,/a/,/u/) we are using for our stimuli, we will measure the vocalic space (over the three corner vowels).
Depending on the initial consonant of each word-trial, we will measure either the Voice Onset Time (for plosives) or the Center of Gravity (for fricatives).
All the plosive consontants will be analyzed together as a single group.
All the fricative consontants will analyzed as another independent group.
statistical_tests We will examine the SOT of trials in relation to the variables Lexical Frequency, Supervision, and Environment. We will inspect our data and remove outliers before testing our hypotheses. We will use linear mixed effect models and use SOT as the dependent variable; Word Frequency (High F. vs Low F.), Supervision (Supervised vs Unsupervised) and Environment (Online vs Onsite) as fixed effects. Initially a minimal structure of random effects (allowed by the experimental design) will be used. Where possible, we will introduce by-subject and by-item random effects (i.e., subject random intercept). Also, we will modify and adjust the model to guarantee the best fit to our data. To identify the best model for our analysis, we will specify various random effects structure and compare models fit with the “Performance” package in R. If any interaction between fixed effects will be detected, that will be further explored by using emmeans package (Tukey HSD test).

The same procedure will be followed for consonant VOT, COG, and vowel space (vowel hyperarticulation). Regarding the latter, we will not conduct a by-item analysis, because this dependent variable can only be calculated by participant.

To investigate whether the two groups of participants (Supervised and Unsupervised) differ in terms of shyness, which could be a confounding factor, we will run an independent samples Bayesian t-test using the individual results of the shyness test as dependent variable.
data_exclusion_criteria We will discard missed or wrong answers - e.g., use of incorrect target name during the picture naming task.
During data pre-processing, we will discard from acoustic analysis those trials that are too noisy or disturbed.

For SOT, VOT and COG, we will only discard values that are 2.5 standard deviation above or below individual mean. Regarding the vowel space analysis, we will also inspect individual distribution and consequently remove outliers. This is important for vowel analysis to ensure that the values fall within the acceptable values for each vowel category.
missing_data_handling If a subject does not complete one of the two sessions (Online/Onsite), that subject will not be included in the analysis. Conversely, if they complete only one of the two tasks (but in both sessions), that subject will be included in the analysis of that task.
exploratory_analyses As part of exploratory analyses, we will introduce the shyness questionnaire individual scores as random intercept of our main models and explore whether shyness influences online and onsite experiment performance.

sample_size_rationale Vowel space:
Power analysis was conducted based on the effect size calculated on vowel space in LF and HF words of previous onsite studies (Munson, 2007; Munson and Solomon, 2004). The effect size in Munson (2007) was ηp2 = 0.45, whereas in Munson & Solomon (2004) was ηp2 = 0.57 (F1). In order to detect the lexical frequency effect on vowel space with 90% of power, we would need 16 participants for within subject conditions (ANOVA within factors, alpha = .05, non-sphericity correction = 1) and 24 (in total) for between conditions (ANOVA between factors, alpha = .05, correlation among repeated measurements = 0.5).
We ran this exploratory F1 power analysis to know the minimum number of participants we need for detecting a difference in vowel space between HF and LF words across conditions. But, given the fact that we are going to use a different statistical test and given that online testing might introduce more variability, we intend to collect data from two groups of 50 participants (in line with Fairs & Strijker, 2021).

Other dependent variables:
The reported power analysis aimed to provide F1 result, indicating the number of participants to measure the vowel space only. Conversely, to decide the number of trials of the other dependent variables, we relied on Brysbaert & Stevens (2018), who suggest that for an effect of 15ms, 1,600 observations per condition are enough to reach 80% of power. Importantly, this number can be distributed across participants and/or trials (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018; see also Keuleers et al., 2012). For instance, Keuleers et al., (2012) reached 80% of power for such an effect of lexical frequency with 40 participants and 40 trials per condition.
The SOT difference between HF and LF is expected to be about 15ms in the reading task (45-50ms in the naming task) (see Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), thus we can rely on the threshold Brysbaert & Stevens (2018) recommend. The studies that explored the effect of lexical frequency on plosive VOT found that LF words have a VOT that is roughly 10 ms longer than HF words (VanDam & Port, 2005). Given that this effect size is 5 ms smaller than that of SOT, the number of observations should be (proportionally) raised to ~2100 within each level (across participants and trials). Since there are no studies on lexical effects in fricatives, we will simply use the same number of trials as for the plosive group.
By recruiting two groups of 50 participants each (100 participants total), we will be able to collect 5,400 observations for the SOT variable, 2,700 observations for the plosive VOT variable, 2,700 for the fricative COG variable in each factor and condition (i.e., 2,700 in the HF-online-supervised condition). This numbers, which are widely above the recommended 1,600 observations, guarantee high statistical power even in the case of some invalid participants and data loss.

[Please note the final number of stimuli was increased to 72 (from the initially planned 54), which further increases the number of observations and enhances the statistical power beyond the more-than-adequate level calculated above.]
stopping_rule We aim to recruit 100 participants to account for possible data loss and have a final sample size of about 92/96 valid participants (~46/48 each group). If we reach 96 valid participants before testing all the 100 participants, we will stop collecting data. If, once all the 100 participants are tested, the number of valid participants is below 46 per group (92 total), we will recruit more participants until reaching at least 46 valid participants per group, allowing us to collect enough data points, as Brysbaert & Stevens (2018) recommend. In fact, 46 participants will allow the collection of ~2480 observations for both consonant groups and of ~4900 observations for the SOT variable.

[Please note the final number of stimuli was increased to 72 (from the initially planned 54), which further increases the number of observations and enhances the statistical power beyond the more-than-adequate level calculated above.]
manipulated_variables We will use bi/three-syllabic HF and LF Spanish words; in each of the two tasks there will be 54 HF and 54 LF words, which will be repeated twice for a total of 216 trials per task [UPDATED 36 HF and 36 LF words repeated three times. 216 total]. The reading task and the naming task will not use the same words to avoid too many repetitions, which would reduce the lexical frequency effect across sessions.
We will use words with the onset being either a plosive (/p/, /t/, /d/) or a fricative consonant (/s/, /f/). There will be 6 words per plosive in the HF condition and 6 in the LF condition (12 words per /p/, /t/, /d/, 36 in total). Due to Spanish orthophonological rules, we can only use two fricatives (/f/ and /s/), so we selected 9 words per fricative in the HF condition and 9 in the LF condition (18 words per /f/ and /s/, 36 in total). Each word will be repeated three times (36 words x 2 consonant groups x 3 repetitions = 216 trials). We will use the corner vowels /i/, /a/, /u/, that will be used to measure participants’ vowel space. From the total number of trials, each vowel will be contained in 72 word-trials of each session and per participant (36 word trials x 2 HF/LF x 3 vowels).

Please read:
[The final design used 36 unique HF and 36 LF words per task, each repeated three times (216 trials total). This adjustment from the initial plan maintained the same total number of trials, thus preserving the intended statistical power.]
study_design_overview We will run two separated tasks: picture naming and reading aloud.
Each one will have a 2x2x2 design: one between-subject factor, Supervision, with two conditions (Supervised and Unsupervised), and two within-subject factors, Word Frequency (High Frequency/Low Frequency) and Environment (Online/Onsite environment). Both Supervised and Unsupervised group of participants will be tested on both the Online and the Onsite conditions on two separated days (total number of sessions: 2). The order of the Environment and of the tasks (Reading and Naming) will be counterbalanced across participants.

[Updated names for publication: Home and Lab (instead of Online and Onsite)].
data_collection_procedures Each participant will be tested in two sessions, one onsite (in the lab) and one online (at home). Depending on the group (Supervised or Unsupervised), the participants will be either supervised by the experimenter in both the online and onsite sessions or not.

The order of the sessions will be counterbalanced across participants. Each session will be carried out on different days and there will be a 6-12 days break between two consecutive sessions. We will use PCIbex (Zehr, Schwarz, 2018), a browser-based tool, to administer the experiment in both the online and the onsite sessions.

In the online sessions, participants will receive a link to the experiment and will be informed that they will be needing a working microphone (either integrated or external) to carry out the tasks. In the onsite sessions, participants will be provided with a headset with microphone.

Participants will be asked to complete the experiment in one go, although they are allowed to have breaks. In both groups and sessions, one screening question will directly query if the participants are alone in a quiet room and if so they will be for the whole duration of the experiment. After that, they will carry out a self-quality check of the recording; if they consider that the output has sufficient quality they will be allowed to proceed.

The Supervised condition will entail the presence of an experimenter who will interact with the participants and inform them the experimenter will be listening and help in case of any problem. For the Supervised group, during the online condition, the interaction will happen via an online conference platform. The same experimenter will be present at both online and onsite (supervised) sessions.

For both Supervised and Unsupervised groups, the same instruction and screening tests will appear on the screen at the beginning of the sessions. Also, the same experimental instruction will be used for both Onsite and Online conditions.

The order of the two tasks will be counterbalanced across participants, half of them will begin with the picture naming task and half with the reading task. In the reading task, the participants will see “+” at the centre of the screen for 500ms at the beginning of each trial, followed by a written word for 2000ms. They will have to read aloud each word before the time runs out and the word disappears. They will not receive any instruction on how to pronounce those words; they will only know that they are being recorded. Each word will appear in three separated blocks and presented in a randomized order.
In the picture naming task, the participants will be first familiarized with the images to ensure naming agreement. Then the main task will follow the same procedure as in the reading task.

In order to account for personal shyness, comfort with supervision and interaction with experimenters, we are going to administer a short questionnaire at the end of the 2nd session, based on Cheek’s (1983) shyness test (see also Cheek & Buss, 1981). By doing so, we will investigate participants’ shyness and determine how they feel regarding supervised and online experiments.
