Full text

Abstract

Remote online experiments are increasingly popular in psycholinguistics, yet their suitability for speech acoustics remains debated. This preregistered study tested whether speech collected online at home reproduces laboratory patterns, and whether an experimenter's presence matters. Ninetysix native Spanish speakers completed picture-naming and reading-aloud tasks once in the lab and once at home (both browser-based), with or without an experimenter. We measured vowel space, plosive voice onset time (VOT) and fricative center of gravity (CoG), and tested lexical frequency effects on each measure across environments and supervision groups.

Compared with the lab, voiceless VOT was shorter at home and CoG was markedly higher, the latter likely reflecting recording artifacts; vowel space was smaller at home in reading, with a similar but non-significant difference in naming. Home-lab agreement of individual speakers' values was good for voiced VOT, moderate for vowel space and voiceless VOT, and poor for CoG. Lexical frequency did not affect VOT or CoG. High-frequency words elicited larger vowel spaces than low-frequency words in naming in both environments, but only at home in reading. Stimulus examination revealed that phonological neighborhood density was confounded with lexical frequency. Exploratory analyses showed that high-density words elicited larger vowel spaces in all conditions and tasks, although the effect was somewhat smaller at home. Critically, experimenter supervision had no effect on any measure in either task.

Thus, unsupervised home recording can capture group-level effects on vowel space, whereas absolute VOT values should not be compared across environments, and CoG is not recommended without controlled recording equipment.

1. Introduction

Although online experimentation dates back to the late '90s (e.g., Givaty et al., 1998; Hecht et al., 1999), its widespread adoption in psycholinguistic research emerged only in recent years, driven by advances in the internet speed, browser quality, and the accessibility of web-based experimental platforms (see Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020). These developments have made online testing increasingly appealing for behavioral research, offering efficient data collection, larger and more diverse samples, and greater statistical power while reducing logistical and financial costs (Henrich et al., 2010; Kimball et al., 2019; Vogt et al., 2021).

Some criticism regarding the time resolution and consistency of online measurementsattributed to differences in internet speed, device quality, operating systems, and browsers (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020; Bridges et al., 2020) has been raised in chronometric research. However, a substantial body of work shows that, despite the above concerns, classical effects, such as lexical frequency and semantic interference, replicate online, with effect sizes comparable to those obtained in the laboratory environment, for both manual responses and vocal response latencies (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020; Bridges et al., 2020; Bürki, 2025; Fairs & Strijkers, 2021; Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026; Vogt et al., 2021). Therefore, online data collection seems to be a suitable setting for psycholinguistic research focusing on manual response and speech latencies.

Crucially, however, speech production is not studied exclusively by measuring naming latencies; acoustic measures -including vowel formants (indexing vowel quality and vowel space expansion), voice onset time (VOT) of plosives, and center of gravity (CoG) of fricatives are central tools for characterising speech production and understanding the cognitive processes that shape it (Burnham et al., 2010; Kalashnikova & Carreiras, 2021; Peng et al., 2010; Piazza et al., 2023; 2025; Rodriguez-Cuadrado et al., 2018; Stoehr et al., 2017; Wikse Barrow et al., 2022; Zheng & Samuel, 2020). Formants represent the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract (Lagefoged, 2006), with the first two formans (F1 and F2) characterizing most of the oral vowels. VOT refers to the time between the release of a plosive consonant and the onset of vocal cord vibration (Liberman et al., 1967 , Lisker & Abramson, 1964), and typically voiced and voiceless plosives display distinct VOT values. CoG represents the frequency-weighted average of a fricative's spectral energy, reflecting articulatory differences in the production of some fricatives, as, for example, /s/ and /f/ (Jongman et al., 2000).

Unlike response latencies and speech onset time (SOT), it is still unclear whether these measures collected remotely, in home or online environments, are comparable to those obtained under controlled laboratory conditions.

In this preregistered study, we tested whether psycholinguistic experiments based on acoustic measures of speech yield similar results when conducted in participants' homes and in the lab. Crucially, both sessions were run on the same online platform (PCIbex), with recordings saved in the same format (WebM). This allowed us to examine within-subject effects of the testing environment while holding the recording software and file format constant. Given that most commercially available microphones now record speech at high quality, and that sound-card differences mainly affect timing rather than recording quality, we did not expect technical factors to change the acoustic measures substantially. Any home-lab differences should therefore mainly reflect the recording environment (e.g., background noise, room reverberation), the microphones used at home, or speaker-related factors, such as a more relaxed speaking style or less psychological stress at home (Stoehr et al., 2023).

Spanish phonetics provides a clear framework for examining our research questions. The Spanish vowel system comprises five monophthongs (/a, e, i, o, u/) with relatively stable formant structure and limited coarticulatory variability compared to English (Bradlow, 1995), making vowel formants a suitable measure of Spanish vowel quality for comparison purposes. Voiceless stops in Spanish (/p, t, k/) are produced with no aspiration (Lisker & Abramson, 1964; Cho & Ladefoged, 1999), whereas voiced stops (/b, d, g/) are produced with prevoicing (Lisker & Abramson, 1964; Rosner et al., 2000; Souganidis et al., 2024), reflected in clearly distinct distributions of positive and negative VOTs, respectively. Fricatives such as /s/ and /f/ vary on the measure of CoG: /s/ typically exhibits a high CoG and concentrated spectral energy, while /f/ shows a diffuse, low-frequency spectrum (Jongman et al., 2000). These measures have been previously investigated as windows into underlying cognitive processes linked to articulatory planning. By leveraging these acoustic features, the present study can assess the viability of online psycholinguistic studies focusing on speech production in varying tasks (reading and naming) and supervision groups (with supervision or without, see below).

1.1. The recording environment

Relocating testing outside the laboratory reduces control over the recording environment.

Variations in microphone type, background noise, room acoustics, and speaker distance across homes can alter the absolute values of acoustic measurements. Accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, a large body of research has evaluated the quality of remote acoustic data collection, including the use of online conferencing platforms such as Zoom (Calder et al., 2025). Zhang et al. (2024), for example, compared laboratory-grade equipment (a portable recorder with a professional headset) with remote methods (a smartphone application and Zoom), all recorded in participants' homes. They found that fundamental frequency was comparable across all conditions, with smartphone recordings most closely approximating the high-quality reference recordings (see also Oganyan et al., 2024). However, lab and home recordings have not been directly compared in detail, and it is uncertain whether high recording quality guarantees comparable acoustic measurements across environments. Moreover, other acoustic features remain untested. Psycholinguistic research is increasingly moving online, with speech researchers being similarly enthusiastic about remote methods. Nevertheless, benchmarking research is needed to systematically delineate both the possibilities and the limitations of online approach to psycholinguistic research on the acoustic measures of speech.

To the best of our knowledge, only one published study has investigated differences in speech measures between online and in-lab environments (Stoehr et al., 2023). Stoehr et al. (2023) conducted a picture naming task in Spanish, Basque, and English, comparing participants' VOT, vowel formants, and vowel duration in a lab (with and without surgical masks) and online home environment. They found that, in both home and lab conditions, L3 English VOT was significantly longer than Spanish and Basque VOT for voiceless plosives, showing that both environments (even with surgical masks) can detect cross-language VOT differences (~12-15 ms). Note that these differences in VOT are already substantial in the lab, indicating that large effect sizes can be replicated online using temporal acoustic features like VOT. However, it is unclear whether smaller effect sizes or within-language manipulations can be replicated with online methods. The authors also observed that VOT was overall shorter in online recordings compared to lab-based. This effect of the environment raises important questions about whether measurements obtained online are directly comparable to those gathered in traditional laboratory environments.

In the same study, Stoehr and colleagues (2023) analyzed the vowel space -determined by the peripheric vowels /a-i-u/ -of Spanish and Basque (combined) to examine whether it differs between home and lab testing environments. Although they found a wider Spanish-Basque vowel space at home than in the lab--suggesting that environment affected absolute acoustic values--it remains unclear whether within-experiment effects on spectral features can be observed in home environment with similar success as in the lab. Lastly, the study did not directly manipulate experimenter presence: participants were unsupervised at home, while an experimenter was present in the lab to ensure protocol compliance, introducing a potential confound between environment and supervision.

1.2. Supervision in home and lab experiments

Another fundamental difference between laboratory and home testing is the experimenter presence. Research on social presence suggests that an observer can both enhance performance, through social facilitation, whereby the presence of others promotes participants' performance (Rosenthal, 1976; Uziel, 2007; Zajonc, 1965), and impair it on tasks requiring executive control, where monitoring induces self-awareness and performance pressure (Belletier et al., 2015; Belletier & Camos, 2018; Palmer et al., 2019).

To our knowledge, the role of experimenter supervision in the expression of psycholinguistic effects has not been directly manipulated for acoustic-phonetic measures, as most of previous studies focused on chronometric outcomes (either reaction time or SOT). For instance, Hilbig (2016), in a lexical decision task, replicated the classical lexical frequency effect (i.e., high frequency words elicit faster responses than low frequency words) in a fully controlled lab setting, web-based experiment in the lab, and a fully web-based experiment conducted online with no experimenter' monitoring. This may suggest that the absence of an experimenter has no impact on the results (similar findings by Ollesch et al., 2006). However, supervision was not manipulated independently of the environment (lab/home), thus confounding the effects of environment and presence of supervision. Piazza et al. (2026) addressed this limitation by crossing environment (home vs. lab conditions) and supervision (supervised vs. unsupervised conditions) in speech-production tasks.

In picture naming, the lexical frequency effect was robust and comparable in both supervised and unsupervised groups (~29-40 ms). In reading aloud, the frequency effect emerged in both groups and environments, except in the home-supervised condition. Importantly, overall, both home-/labunsupervised conditions yielded the largest effect sizes, suggesting that experimenter presence may subtly dampen frequency effects, possibly via increased self-monitoring, and that these effects are more salient in home environments, where supervision might be experienced as unusual. Supervision can therefore modulate small psycholinguistic effects, manifested in smaller differences in SOT (i.e., planning times) between high frequency (HF) and low frequency (LF) words.

It remains uncertain whether dampening effects of supervision extend to spectro-temporal features of speech sounds, such as formants, VOT, or CoG. By crossing supervision with environment, the present design examines whether differences in speech acoustics between home and lab environments are due to the physical setting or the presence of an experimenter.

1.3. Lexical frequency effect and speech quality

The lexical frequency effectone of the most robust effects in psycholinguisticsis characterized by faster recognition or naming of HF words as compared to LF ones. It has been found in various experimental designs, in both written and pictured word recognition (e.g., reading aloud or picture naming; Zipf, 1929; see Brysbaert et al., 2011 for a review). The effect is generally attributed to more efficient lexical access: frequently encountered words have higher resting activation levels, making them easier to retrieve (Navarrete et al., 2006). Its ubiquity and reliability have established the frequency effect as a standard benchmark for validating new methods, and recent studies have demonstrated its successful replication online for response latencies (Bürki, 2025; Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026).

Beyond response latencies, lexical frequency has been reported to influence the acoustic quality of speech (Aylett & Turk, 2006; Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004; Tomaschek et al., 2014). For instance, Kawamoto et al. (1999) and Gahl (2008) observed shorter duration of the initial phoneme in HF words as compared to LF words. Munson (2007) and Munson & Solomon (2004) found that vowels in HF words were produced more centrally than in LF words, resulting in smaller vowel spaces in HF words. VanDam and colleagues (2009) and VanDam and Port (2005) reported shorter VOT of voiceless plosives in HF than LF words in word reading (~11ms; see Stuart-Smith et al., 2015; Yao, 2009 for similar results in spontaneous speech). Taken together, these findings suggest that word frequency impacts production beyond speech planning, affecting the acoustic quality of speech sounds, where high frequency words produced less "pricesely": with shorter onsets, shorter VOTs and reduced vowel spaces. While our primary aim is to examine differences (if any) in acoustic speech production measures between lab and home environments and based on supervisor presence, we use the lexical frequency effect as a benchmark to test whether it is detected with comparable effect size across environments and supervision conditions.

2. The current study

In this study, we compared vowel space, plosives' VOT, and fricatives' CoG in speech production tasks collected in the lab versus at home (within-participants) environment and with or without experimenter supervision (between-participants), in two tasks: picture naming and reading aloud.

This preregistered design and hypotheses (available here https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YX3E7) forms part of a wider project on online psycholinguistic methods, whose first installment examined SOT (Piazza et al., 2026); the present study examines the spectral and temporal properties of speech sounds.

Our primary aim is to assess differences in the acoustic measures of speech, in reading and naming, when collected at home, as compared to the lab (both online), and whether the presence of supervision affects them. More specifically, we asked, first, whether the acoustic measures of speech overall differ between home and lab environments, possibly arising from microphone, computer, and background-noise differences; and second, whether supervision modulates any of those measures or interacts with the environment. Since the home sessions and the unsupervised group both entail less experimental control, this least controlled condition (unsupervised-home) might diverge most (as with SOT, see Piazza et al., 2026). Crucially, and thirdly, regardless of differences between the environments, we examined whether within-subject psycholinguistic effects remain similarly detectable in both environments and supervision groups. We used lexical frequency effect and assessed whether the magnitude and the direction on its effect on the acoustic measures of speech differed between environments and supervision groups (Hameau et al., 2021; Mousikou & Rastle, 2015; Sadat et al., 2014; Scarborough, 2013; Wright et al., 2004).

Based on previous studies (Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004; VanDam et al., 2009; VanDam & Port, 2005), we expected significant lexical frequency effects, with LF words being produced with larger vowel spaces and longer VOT (with stronger effects in voiceless, cf VanDam et al., 2009) than HF words. Critically, we expected those effects to be significant in both environments (lab and home), with no Environment × Frequency interaction. The environment might affect the absolute values, with vowel spaces being smaller and VOTs being longer in the lab than at home (Stoehr et al., 2023), possibly because the formal laboratory environment induces more pronunciation effort and psychological stress than the more relaxed home environment. Yet, we expected that the magnitude of the lexical frequency effect would remain similar in both environments. We additionally measured fricatives' CoG to explore their values between environments and supervision groups, and, for the first time, to our knowledge, we explored whether they were modulated by lexical frequency. Because higher-frequency words are typically produced with reduced articulatory effort (Lindblom, 1990; Aylett & Turk, 2004), we predicted that high lexical frequency would shift fricative CoG toward more central values.

Two tasks -reading aloud and picture naming (hence naming and reading) -that typically elicit sizable lexical frequency effects were selected for the current study. Naming yields larger frequency effect sizes than reading aloud (Mousikou & Rastle, 2015), letting us test the sensitivity of our environments to detect strong and weaker effects within the same participants. It is possible, in fact, that home recordings are suitable for relatively big effect sizes but not for small ones. Finally, the supervision manipulation is aimed at separating two factors confounded in most of previous research: presence of supervision in the lab and its absence at home. If supervision induces performance pressure, the unsupervised group would show amplified acoustic measures (larger vowel space, longer VOT, higher CoG) and possibly larger differences between HF and LF words (Piazza et al., 2026). Results will clarify whether home-lab differences should be attributed to the environment or to the supervision, and will provide a practical benchmark for collecting speech production data online.

3. Method

>Method

3.1. Participants

One-hundred and two participants without diagnosed reading disorders and with normal/corrected to normal vision were recruited from the BCBL participant database to take part in the study. Five were excluded because they did not complete both sessions, and one was excluded because of recording issues. The final sample size was 96. Participants were randomly assigned to the supervised (N = 47, Mage = 29.25, SD = 5.79; 33 Women/14 Men) and the unsupervised group (N = 49, Mage = 28.96, SD = 6.20, 34 Women/15 Men). Based on the effect sizes reported in previous research for vowel space expansion (ηₚ² = 0.12-0.65; Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004), we estimated that to reach 90% power for between-subject comparison, we needed 24 participants. For other variables, following Brysbaert & Stevens, (2018), an effect of ~15 ms would require about 1,600 observations per condition to reach 80% power. With 96 participants, our design yielded more than 5,100 observations for VOT and CoG in each condition (e.g., HF-home-supervised). These observation counts, which exceed the recommended threshold, provide high statistical power even accounting for potential data loss or effects smaller than 15ms (see detailed power analysis description in pre-registration (https://osf.io/yx3e7), and Data availability and Supplementary Material for details and the complete power analysis). In order to account for personality differences that could influence competence under supervision, we administered a 13-item questionnaire on personality type (Melchior & Cheek, 1990) to determine, for each participant, whether they tended to be more or less shy and show inhibition in the presence of others. Shyness was chosen as a straightforward measure of social comfort that plausibly can influence supervised speech performance, and it correlates with related constructs such as social anxiety and extraversion (Cheek & Buss, 1981). We used the ζ-Overlapping test, in R (Pastore, 2018; Pastore & Calcagnì, 2019; Perugini et al., 2024) with permutation-based inference to compare density distribution of the two groups and estimate exact p-values. This method is assumption-free and computes the exact probability of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one observed (Perugini et al., 2024). Comparing shyness scores did not yield a significant difference between supervision groups (p = .072). All participants signed an informed consent form before starting the experimental procedure, and the study was approved by the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) Ethics Committee. Participants were paid 18 euros for taking part in the study.

3.2. Material

We used Spanish di/tri-syllabic HF and LF words. In each task (naming and reading), participants encountered 36 unique HF and 36 unique LF words, repeated three times. This final count of unique stimuli differs from the preregistration (which specified 54 words repeated twice) due to challenges in identifying a sufficient number of words meeting all selection criteria (specified below). The total number of trials was kept identical though, maintaining planned statistical power.

Words had CVCV, CVCVCV, or CVCCVCV structure. Word onsets were either a plosive (/d/, /p/, /t/) 1 or a fricative consonant (/s/, /f/). There were 12 words per plosive per frequency condition (12 words x 3 plosives x 2 frequency levels x 3 repetitions = 216 trials). There were 18 words per fricative per frequency condition (18 words x 2 fricatives x 2 frequency levels x 3 repetitions = 216 trials). The vowels in the second position of the words were /a/, /i/, /u/ (for example, tarta, 'cake', piso, 'apartment'; for a complete list of words, see the OSF repository) and were used to draw the vowel triangle and measure participants' vowel space over the three corner vowels of Spanish. Word stress was always on the first syllable, and the presence of a graphic accent (for the reading task, e.g., página, 'page') was counterbalanced across LF and HF conditions. There were 24 words per target vowel per frequency level, repeated 3 times (3 vowels x 12 words x 2 frequency levels x 3 repetitions = 216 trials per environment). Word frequencies for the Spanish HF and LF words were obtained from the EsPal database (Duchon et al., 2013), which provides comprehensive lexical statistics for Spanish words. The naming and the reading tasks did not include the same words to avoid potential reduction in the frequency effect due to repetition. The words used in naming were all concrete whereas some abstract words were used in reading. The number of concrete and abstract words in reading was matched between the conditions (HF and LF). Pictures were chosen from the Multipic database (Duñabeitia et al., 2018) and, when not available there, from freely accessible pictures on the internet, (see the Data and Code Availability section for the link to the pictures). They were colored 300x300 pixel pictures presented on a white background.

1 We included both voiced and voiceless plosives to improve generalizability of the findings and because previously observed effects on voiceless plosive VOT in English (e.g., VanDam et al., 2009), which are aspirated, may differ from those in Spanish, where voiceless plosives are unaspirated.

For words in each task, we compared the number of letters and syllables between HF and LF words. We also collected subjective ratings on word imageability and visual complexity (in naming), on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (completely) from 10 native Spanish speakers (5 female). In all cases, the ζ-Overlapping results showed no significant differences between HF and LF words (see Data availability and Supplementary Material).

3.3. Procedure

Participants in both supervised or unsupervised groups completed two counterbalanced sessions, one conducted in the laboratory and one at home (both online), scheduled 6-12 days apart. In each session, participants performed both naming and reading tasks, in counterbalanced order. In the supervised group, participants were accompanied by the same experimenter in both environment: when in the lab, they were welcomed and seated in an experimental booth equipped with a camera and microphone for technical assistance; at home, they remained observed by the experimenter via Zoom, with their camera and microphone active throughout the session. In both contexts, once the task began, participants could no longer see the experimenter, and all instructions were presented on full screen to ensure similar conditions. The experimenter did not provide any task-specific guidance, to ensure similar instructions in the supervised and unsupervised groups.

Participants in the unsupervised group completed the tasks without supervisor guidance. At home, they accessed the study via a link, provided in an email, and performed both tasks within the allotted day (whenever it was more convenient for them); in the lab, they entered a booth where the task was displayed on a laptop's screen, without an experimenter or camera present. When collecting data in the lab (for both supervised and unsupervised groups), we recorded participants using a Sennheiser HMD 280 Pro headset with a dynamic microphone (-47 dB, 50-13,500 Hz). In the home environment, participants were permitted to use any available microphone, including both laptop-integrated and externally mounted devices. Prior to the start of the experiment, they were asked to record a short sentence, play it back, and confirm that the audio quality was satisfactory before proceeding. Participants reported which microphone and browser they used.

Reading and naming tasks were implemented in PennController for Ibex (Zehr & Schwarz, 2018), a JavaScript-based platform for browser experiments. Recordings were saved in WebM format and converted to WAV offline. In each task, each trial began with a fixation cue ("+++") for 500 ms, followed by the target word or image for 2000 ms. Participants were asked to respond aloud as soon as the stimulus appeared and while it was displayed on the screen. To ensure full capture of the response, recording continued for an additional 500 ms after stimulus offset. Each stimulus was presented three times, in a pseudorandomized order such that words sharing the same plosive onset did not appear on two consecutive trials, to minimize phonological clustering. Each task lasted about 20 minutes. Finally, participants completed Cheek and Melchior's (1990) shyness questionnaire. Further methodological details about the online recording procedure are reported in Piazza et al. (2026).

3.4. Data processing

All the recordings were phonetically forced aligned to their transcription using easyalign (Goldman, 2011) and phoneme boundaries were manually corrected when necessary. Thus, all target sounds were marked in TextGrid files and extracted by custom scripts in PRAAT software (Boersma & Weenink, 2001). Then, we computed our dependent variables: vowel space expansion, VOT for plosives, and CoG for fricatives.

Vowel onset was defined as the first glottal pulse showing a clear higher-formant (notably F2) structure in the spectrogram, and offset as the point at which intensity clearly dropped and the formants became less defined at the transition to the following segment. We examined the first (F1) and second (F2) formant values of the /a/, /i/, /u/ vowel midpoints to calculate vowel space with the package PhonR in R (R Core Team, 2012.

Vowel space area (VSA) was computed as the area of the triangle formed by these three vowels in the F1×F2 plane, using the Shoelace formula: VSA = 0.5

A larger vowel space indicates more peripheral corner vowels Prior to the vowel space calculation, participants' F1 and F2 values were transformed following the Bark method to reduce between-speaker differences in formant estimations due to anatomical differences in the vocal tract (Traunmüller, 1990). Fricative onset was defined as the appearance of aperiodic high-frequency frication noise, and offset as its cessation at the onset of the following segment. CoG of /f/, /s/ consonants was extracted from the entire duration of each fricative using the Praat script zero-crossings-and-spectral-moments (v.1.3; Elvira-Garcia, 2014). Prior to the spectral analysis, a Hann band-pass filter was applied (1,000-11,000 Hz, smoothing 100 Hz). CoG was then calculated from the power spectrum (power = 2) using Praat's built-in function and a logarithmic transformation was applied to make the two consonants comparable. VOT was measured manually for the plosives /p/, /t/, and /d/ (among the most extensively studied plosives in psycholinguistic research). For voiceless plosives, the onset was defined as the release burst of the plosive and the offset as the onset of voicing in the following vowel, identified by the appearance of the first formant (F1). For the voiced plosive (/d/), prevoicing was measured as negative VOT, with the offset VOT defined as the voicing onset of vowel following the burst. Voiced plosives in Spanish can be produced as devoiced (i.e., with positive VOT) incidentally (e.g., Souganidis et al., 2024; Stoehr et al., 2023 Stoehr et al., , 2025)). Devoiced plosives were discarded from further analyses. As VOT values for voiced plosives were negative and those for voiceless plosives positive, absolute values were taken to allow a uniform treatment of VOT as an index of articulatory precision across voicing categories, irrespective of direction, to allow consistent comparison between environments and supervision groups (Baayen et al., 2008; see Lo & Andrews, 2015 for discussion). Note that in Spanish voiceless plosives are strictly positive whereas voiced plosives are typically negative (Lisker & Abramson, 1964), which allows us to use the absolute values to regroup the two groups. Smaller values would indicate less precise articulation. A logarithmic transformation was then applied to the absolute values to normalize the distribution.

All missed and mispronounced words, plosive-initial voiced words produced without prevoicing, and responses with excessive noise were discarded from the analysis. For each task separately, we removed all responses exceeding 2.5 standard deviations above or below the participant's individual mean (by session) for each variable (in line with previous research using acoustic measures, e.g., Piazza et al., 2025). In the naming task, missed responses, mispronunciations, responses with excessive background noise, and trials exceeding ±2.5 SD from the participant's mean represented 14.07% of trials for vowels, 8.80% for VOT, and 9.95% for CoG; they were all discarded from further analyses. In the reading task, the exclusion rates were 9.89% for vowels, 4.13% for VOT, and 1.60% for CoG. No significant exclusion rate differences were found across conditions (all p-values > .05).

3.5. Statistical analysis

The results of the naming and reading tasks were analyzed separately. For each acoustic feature, we fit linear mixed-effects models with sum-coded Frequency (within-subject HF/LF, contr.sum -1/1); Environment (within-subject home/lab, contr.sum -1/1), Supervision (betweensubject supervised/unsupervised, contr.sum -1/1) and their interactions as fixed effects (see specific formulas in the Results section). The models for VOT and CoG, respectively, included voicing (/p, t/ vs. /d/, treatment coded, reference: voiced) and fricative (/f/ vs. /s/, treatment coded, reference: /f/) as additional fixed factors. The preregistration planned to start from a minimal random-effects structure and compare alternative structures with the performance package. We departed from this plan because building up from a minimal structure risks omitting random slopes required by the design, which inflates Type I error (Barr et al., 2013). Fully maximal structures, on the other hand, are often overparameterized and fail to converge. We therefore followed the parsimonious approach of Bates et al. (2015). We started from a reduced model including only Frequency (plus voicing or fricative), with by-subject and by-item random slopes. Random slopes explaining less than 1% of the variance in a principal component analysis of the random-effects structure were then removed (see Data availability and Supplementary Material for details).

After finalizing the random structure, as preregistered, for each dependent variable we fit a linear mixed-effects model with Frequency, Environment, Supervision and their interactions as fixed effects (plus voicing in the VOT models and fricative in the CoG models), with the random structure selected as described above. We then tested whether adding the number of repetitions (NUM_REP; numeric: 0, 1, 2) improved model fit, and retained it only when it did, based on the fit indices of the performance package (AIC, BIC, marginal/conditional R², RMSE; Lüdecke et al., 2021). The steps to get to the final models can be viewed on the R Markdown available in the OSF repository.

As preregistered, we report the full model, including all interactions, for every measure. The significance of main effects and interactions was assessed with type II Wald χ² tests (car package;

Fox & Weisberg, 2019). Significant interactions were followed up with pairwise comparisons (emmeans package; Lenth et al., 2020), Holm-corrected instead of the preregistered Tukey HSD, which applies no correction when a single two-level contrast is tested. Our research questions concerned both the effect of the environment and whether the lexical frequency effect held in each environment and supervision group. We therefore also report the Frequency effect (and, in the exploratory analyses, the PND effect) within each Environment and Supervision condition as the model estimate with its 95% CI and Cohen's d. These per-condition effects are simple effects estimated from the full model and they describe the size and direction of the effect in each condition, but they are not tests of differences between conditions, which are assessed only by the interaction terms. For this reason, we report them without p-values and do not contrast individual conditions unless the corresponding interaction is significant; the Holm-corrected tests of the per-condition effects are provided in the supplementary material.

4.2.4. Exploratory Analysis: Phonological Neighborhood Density.

Vowel space. Phonological Neighborhood Density (PND) is known to affect the quality of speech production: words with high PND yield wider vowel spaces than with low PND words (Munson & Solomon, 2004; Wright, 2004). Therefore, after observing the unexpected direction of lexical frequency effect on vowel space expansion (HF words showing larger vowel space than LF words), we explored whether the effect was not partially due to higher PND in HF words and lower PND in LF words. In our stimuli, PND and frequency were correlated, although weakly (Naming task: Spearman's r = .33; Reading task: Spearman's r = .24). We split the words into High and Low PND (a factor we called cat_PND) based on the EsPal database (Duchon et al., 2013) and re-computed the vowel space measure separately for High and Low PND words. We followed the same procedure as we employed for the analysis of Lexical Frequency, including the main models and follow-up analyses, all of them being exploratory. 4.4. Exploratory Analysis: Home-Lab Agreement

To assess whether speakers performance was comparable across environments, we computed each participant's mean for each measure and task in the lab and at home, and estimated their agreement with two-way, single-measure intraclass correlations (McGraw & Wong, 1996), ICC(C,1), which quantifies consistency and ignores a constant home-lab shift, and ICC(A,1), which quantifies absolute agreement (see supplementary material for the results of 95% CIs from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of participants and plots). Voiced /d/ and voiceless /p,t/ were analysed separately given the different effects of Environment. Following Koo and Li (2016), agreement was moderate for vowel space (naming / reading: ICC(C,1) = .52 / .57, ICC(A,1) = .52 / .56), moderate to poor for voiceless VOT (.63 / .51 and .57 / .45), good for /d/ prevoicing (.77 / .81 and .78 / .81), and poor for CoG (/s/: .44 / .42 and .39 / .36). For /f/, home values were essentially unrelated to lab values (ICC(C,1) = .04 / .06; ICC(A,1) = .03 / .04). For vowel space and /d/, the two ICCs were nearly identical, so disagreement reflected speaker-specific variability rather than a common shift; for voiceless VOT and /s/, absolute agreement was lower than consistency, reflecting the home-lab shift (Table 10; full results and figures in the supplementary material). Because the two sessions took place on different days, these values also include day-to-day variability and are a lower bound on the agreement attributable to the recording environment. 5. Discussion

This study evaluated the reliability of online experiments for speech production research focusing on the acoustic measures of speech. Ninety-six Spanish speakers completed a picture naming and a reading aloud task once in the laboratory and once at home, with or without an experimenter's supervision. We compared three acoustic features: vowel space expansion, VOT of plosives and CoG of fricatives. First, and primarily, we asked whether these acoustic measures differ between the home and lab environments and between supervised and unsupervised groups. Second, we asked whether a within-experiment manipulation, lexical frequency, modulates the acoustic measures to a similar extent across environments and groups (that is, if absolute values shift but psycholinguistic effects can still be detected). Validating online acoustic measurement is timely: while the reliability of web-based chronometric measures has now been extensively documented (e.g., Bürki, 2025; Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026), whether the spectral and temporal properties of speech itself can be equally captured outside the laboratory remains largely open (Stoehr et al., 2023).

Below, we discuss the two research questions in turn, each followed by an interim conclusion, and then consider the implications and limitations for remote speech production research.

5.1. Acoustic differences between environments and supervision groups.

level and within-speaker effects (Section 5.2) better than they reproduce a given speaker's vowel space.

Plosive VOT. In both tasks, VOT was significantly shorter at home than in the lab. Follow-up exploratory analyses showed that this difference, however, was restricted to voiceless plosives (naming: lab 26 ms vs. home 23 ms; reading: 25 ms vs. 23 ms), whereas the prevoicing of /d/ did not differ between environments.

Similarly to the results for vowel space, the direction matched our preregistered expectation of shorter VOTs in less controlled sessions. Although this result should be interpreted cautiously, because the stimuli had an unbalanced number of voiced and voiceless consonants (/p, t/ vs. /d/) and the analysis is exploratory, it replicates and extends Stoehr et al. (2023), who examined voiceless plosives (/p, t, k/) and similarly found longer VOTs in the lab than in home recordings of Spanish and Basque speakers. Importantly, Stoehr and colleagues compared lab recordings (not browser-based) with web recordings, whereas in our study both environments were browser-based, yet we still observed longer lab VOTs for voiceless plosives.

Thus, the effect is unlikely to be due to the browser or recording platform. It might instead reflect the microphones used at home. Additional analyses revealed that the home-lab difference did not differ between participants using a mounted versus a laptop-internal microphone at home, even when voiceless plosives were considered alone (see Data availability and Supplementary Material). However, both types are typically consumer-grade devices, unlike the Sennheiser headset used in the lab, and they may capture the weak, short-lag VOT of Spanish voiceless plosives less well than the strong periodic energy of prevoicing, which would shorten the measured VOT for voiceless plosives only.

Alternatively, the difference may reflect contextual factors such as the more familiar, relaxed home environment, consistent with the smaller vowel spaces at home. If this is the case, since experimenter supervision had no effect, any such influence is more likely tied to the place itself than to being observed. At the speaker level, voiceless VOT was only moderately to poorly preserved across environments (ICC(A,1) = .57/.45 for naming/reading), whereas /d/ prevoicing was well preserved (.78/.81; Section 4.4). Absolute VOT values should therefore not be compared across home and lab recordings, and analyses of voiceless VOT should remain within one environment until further validation is available.

Fricative CoG. CoG was strikingly higher at home than in the lab for both /f/ and /s/, in both tasks (Cohen's d = 0.39-0.40), and the shift was much larger for /f/, whose CoG almost doubled at home (e.g., naming: 1,823 Hz in the lab vs. 3,641 Hz at home). Together with the large variability of home values (Figures 3 and 6; Table 1), this pattern points to a recording-condition artifact rather than a genuine change in participants' articulation. Fricative spectral measures such as CoG are among the acoustic measures most affected by the recording device, with built-in computer microphones yielding systematically shifted (higher) CoG values (Sanker et al., 2021). Alternatively, broadband high-frequency noise present in home environments, such as laptop fans or ambient sound, would shift the spectral CoG upward regardless of the phoneme, and more so for a weak fricative such as /f/, whose own energy is low relative to the noise. As for VOT, the home-lab difference in CoG did not differ between participants who used a mounted or a laptop microphone at home. It was also already present among Chrome users (69/81 participants for /f/ and 62/81 for /s/), with the same direction among users of other browsers (see Data availability and Supplementary Material), so it cannot be attributed to participants using a different browser at home than in the lab. Absolute CoG values are therefore not comparable across recording environments.

Moreover, a speaker's CoG in one environment hardly predicted their CoG in the other, as the homelab agreement was poor for /s/ (ICC(A,1) = .39/.36 for naming/reading) and essentially absent for /f/ (ICC(A,1) = .03/.04; Section 4.4), so home recordings did not even preserve the ranking of speakers.

Supervision. The clearest and most practically relevant finding is the consistent absence of a supervision effect. In all three acoustic measures, both tasks, and both environments, supervised and unsupervised participants produced comparable values, and Supervision did not interact with Environment or Frequency in any model. This suggests that neither social facilitation nor monitoringinduced performance anxiety affected the spectral or temporal properties of speech production.

This contrasts with our preregistered expectation (based on Zajonc, 1965; Belletier et al., 2015) that supervision would modulate the acoustic measures and the frequency effect but is consistent with prior work showing supervision-independent replication of lexical effects on response times (Hilbig, 2016; Piazza et al., 2026). The present study extends this result, for the first time, to acousticphonetic measures. Notably, even the home-supervised condition, in which monitoring via webcam might have created a tension between domestic comfort and awareness of being observed, produced data statistically similar to the other conditions. For researchers, this has practical consequences: online supervision via webcam remains a viable option to ensure protocol compliance without a laboratory visit, but it can also be dropped without compromising the quality of the acoustic data.

To summarize, the recording environment affected all three measures, but to different degrees and plausibly for different reasons, whereas supervision affected none. Vowel space and voiceless VOT were slightly reduced at home; these small differences are compatible with a more relaxed speaking style. Fricative CoG, in contrast, was substantially shifted at home, most likely by the recording equipment (consumer-grade microphones at home vs. a high-quality microphone in the lab) and environmental noise. At the level of individual speakers, home-lab agreement was moderate for vowel space and voiceless VOT, good for /d/ prevoicing, and very poor for CoG (Section 4.4, Table 10). Home recordings preserve group-level and within-speaker patterns better than they reproduce a given speaker's values. Absolute values should therefore not be pooled or compared across environments without caution, especially for CoG, whereas the presence of an experimenter, in the lab or via webcam, is not needed to obtain comparable acoustic data.

5.2. Lexical frequency effects across measures

with a somewhat reduced effect size that should be considered in power analyses. Since this analysis was exploratory, future research manipulating PND across tasks and conditions is needed to confirm these findings.

VOT and CoG. Lexical frequency did not modulate VOT or CoG in any task, environment or supervision group. Previous frequency effects on VOT have been reported for English voiceless plosives (VanDam et al., 2009; VanDam & Port, 2005), which are aspirated with long-lag VOT.

Spanish voiceless plosives, however, are unaspirated and show relatively little VOT variability, making them a less informative test case. By contrast, voiced stops in true-voicing languages like Spanish can be produced with a wide range of VOT values (e.g., Colina, 2020; Hualde, 2025; Rosner et al., 2000; Souganidis et al., 2024; Stoehr et al., 2025) and may therefore be more sensitive to frequency effects (see the exploratory analysis of /d/ in the Supplementary Material). Future research should explicitly manipulate voicing and frequency to clarify how language-specific phonetic properties interact with lexical variables in VOT production. On the other hand, this is the first investigation of lexical frequency effects on fricative CoG to our knowledge. We hypothesized that speakers would produce HF words with a more central CoG, but the effect did not reach significance in either task; given the size of the environment artifact, a small psycholinguistic modulation would be difficult to detect at home. Because these null results held in the lab as well as at home, they do not speak against home recordings; rather, they indicate that lexical frequency is not a suitable benchmark for these two measures in Spanish.

The frequency effect on vowel space in naming and the (exploratory) PND effect in both tasks emerged in all environments and supervision groups, although the PND effect was somewhat smaller at home. Frequency effects were absent for VOT and CoG in both environments, so they could not serve as a benchmark for these measures. Overall, lexical frequency proved a weaker and less consistent probe of acoustic variation than phonological neighborhood density, and a null or reversed frequency effect on a given measure cannot, by itself, be taken as evidence that home recording failed.

5.3. Limitations

All participants completed both a laboratory and a home session and may thus have become familiar with the protocol. Although the order was counterbalanced, we assessed the PND effect (the strongest effect we observed) on vowel space at home, restricting the sample to participants who completed their home session before any laboratory exposure (N = 48): the effect remained significant in both tasks (naming: t(48) = 8.85; reading: t(48) = 6.67; both p < .001; Supplementary Material), also when restricted to the unsupervised group (N = 26), suggesting that the validity of home recordings does not depend on prior laboratory familiarity. Additionally, to be as close as possible to realistic remote recording, the home equipment was not controlled and participants could use any device, so we cannot separate the contributions of microphones and room acoustics to the Environment effects. Future studies could address this by providing participants with a standard headset.

6. Conclusion

This study used a picture naming and a reading aloud task to test whether speech acoustics recorded online at home, with or without an experimenter, reproduce laboratory patterns. The answer is measure-specific (Table 10 summarizes our recommendations by measure). Compared with the lab, vowel spaces were slightly smaller at home (significantly so in reading only), voiceless VOT was shorter, and fricative CoG was markedly higher, the latter most likely reflecting recording artifacts. Experimenter supervision had no effect on any measure, in the lab or at home.

Psycholinguistic effects on vowel space were detected in both environments: lexical frequency in naming and, in exploratory analyses, phonological neighborhood density in both tasks, with a slightly smaller effect at home. Lexical frequency did not affect VOT or CoG in either environment.

These findings suggest that, for some speech production studies, unsupervised home recording is a viable alternative to the lab. Vowel measures are suitable for group-level and withinspeaker comparisons in within-subject designs, although individual vowel spaces agreed only moderately across environments. VOT should be compared within, not across, recording environments, and voiced and voiceless plosives may be affected differently. Fricative CoG is not recommended for remote studies without controlled equipment. Remote paradigms can therefore support speech production research, provided that the choice of acoustic measure takes into account its sensitivity to recording conditions.

Vowel space. Vowel space was smaller at home than in the lab in both tasks; the difference reached significance in reading (lab-home = 0.61 Bark², Cohen's d = 0.15) and went in the same direction only numerically in naming. This direction is in line with our preregistered expectation that less controlled sessions would elicit less hyperarticulated vowels, although the reduction emerged as an overall Environment effect rather than specifically in the home-unsupervised condition. A more relaxed speaking style at home, with less articulatory effort, therefore, could explain the reduction we observed, whereas the formal laboratory environment may induce more careful, hyperarticulated speech. It is opposite, however, to the wider Spanish-Basque vowel space observed at home by Stoehr et al. (2023). Differences in recording setup may have contributed to the discrepancy between the two studies. In Stoehr et al. (2023), lab sessions were recorded with a dedicated recorder, whereas online sessions were recorded through a web-based tool on participants' own devices.

Recording software and file format therefore differed between their two environments. In our study, both sessions were recorded through the same browser-based platform (PCIbex) and saved in the same format (WebM), so differences in recording software or file format cannot explain our Environment effect; only the microphones differed (a headset in the lab, participants' own devices at home). Home recordings were also more variable; the standard deviation of vowel space was larger at home than in the lab for both naming (home: M = 8.46 Bark², SD = 3.24 vs. lab: M = 9.01 Bark², SD = 2.39) and reading (home: M = 8.43 Bark², SD = 3.28 vs. lab: M = 9.07 Bark², SD = 2.26; see Table 1), in line with previous research showing that online experiments typically introduce greater variability (Bürki, 2025). Importantly, the Environment effect was small relative to the differences between speakers. In fact, in all vowel models, most of the variance was accounted for by participants (R²c ≥ .95 vs. R²m ≤ .06; Tables 2, 5, 6 and 9). However, speakers' vowel spaces were only moderately preserved across environments (ICC(A,1) = .52 / .56 for naming / reading; Section 4.4). Together with the larger variability at home, this indicates that home recordings preserve group-Vowel space. In naming, lexical frequency modulated vowel space in both environments and supervision groups, with similar effect sizes at home and in the lab (Cohen's d = 0.14 and 0.19). Surprisingly, however, HF words were produced with wider vowel spaces than LF words, contrary to our hypothesis (Munson, 2007; Munson & Solomon, 2004) but in line with Tomaschek et al. (2014).

In reading, the effect was very small (d = 0.04) and was present at home but not in the lab, contrary to our preregistered expectation of comparable effects in both environments. The larger frequency effect in naming is in line with the greater role of frequency in lexical access in picture naming (Mousikou & Rastle, 2015). Since the effect emerged in naming in all recording conditions, the vowelspace measure collected at home appears sensitive enough to detect within-subject psycholinguistic effects of this size.

Phonological neighborhood density.

The unexpected direction of the frequency effect led us to examine the stimuli, which revealed that HF words tended to have more phonological neighbors than LF words (Spearman's r = .33 and .24 in naming and reading). High-density neighborhoods impose greater phonological competition during production, driving speakers toward more peripheral, hyperarticulated vowels to maximize contrast (Scarborough, 2013; Wright et al., 2004; Hameau et al., 2021), indicating that the direction of a frequency effect on vowel space likely depends on how frequency and density covary in the stimuli. Accordingly, our exploratory analyses showed that High-PND words elicited wider vowel spaces than Low-PND words in both tasks, environments and supervision groups, with larger effects (Cohen's d = 0.35 and 0.34 in naming and reading) and more variance explained by the fixed effects (R²m) than for frequency. The PND effect, however, was smaller at home than in the lab in both tasks (naming: d = 0.31 vs. 0.39; reading: d = 0.30 vs. 0.38). This reduction parallels the smaller vowel spaces at home discussed above.

Accordingly, if speakers hyperarticulate less at home, there may also be less room for density-driven expansion. Nevertheless, the effect remained robust at home, even without supervision, indicating that small-to-moderate psycholinguistic effects on vowel space can be measured remotely, although
